title: Poundland emergency, fireworks nuisance, and online consumer protection
label: 3 November 2026 · Consumer protection evidence session
summary: Ministers and regulators told the Committee they are urgently engaging to try to save thousands of Poundland jobs after takeover turmoil, are analysing record responses to a fireworks consultation and plan legal changes, and are pressing ahead with new rules and enforcement on misleading online pricing, marketplaces and unsafe products while work continues on payments protections, e-bikes and furniture safety.

chapters.title: Poundland's crisis and urgent government engagement
chapters.takeaway: Ministers are urgently pressing Poundland owners to protect 12,000 jobs and suppliers while facts about bids, debt and director actions remain disputed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We begin with Poundland: 12,000 jobs and about 30,000 in the supply chain are at risk. Minister, how confident are you that the business can be saved?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: This is a very worrying time for workers and communities. We're talking closely with Poundland, Gordon Brothers and USDAW the union, meeting them this week, and pressing for reassurance that jobs and suppliers are prioritised.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There are tight timelines: Poundland filed a notice on 29 October (a 10‑day notice of intention) and was briefly shown as dissolved at Companies House. Gordon Brothers and Poundland have separate meetings this week — what's the nature of this Thursday deadline?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: The 10‑day notice period was filed on 29 October; that doesn't automatically mean administration. We need to understand the company's position when officials and ministers meet them.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: About 200 stores have closed since Gordon Brothers took over; roughly half by Gordon Brothers and half by Poundland management. Do you know how much Gordon Brothers has already taken from the business?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: Media reports vary. We're pressing the company directly to establish the facts and to stress how important it is to protect employees and suppliers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A fully funded offer to buy the business is reported to exist. Has the Government seen it?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: We won't comment on bids or interfere in commercial choices. If there are viable offers, Gordon Brothers needs to explain its decisions, especially to protect jobs.

turns.speaker: Dan Aldridge
turns.text: Constituents and workers have already sacrificed to turn Poundland around: there are reports of an £8.4m profit and an 11% sales rise. What assurance can you give that Government will hold owners to account and support staff?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: Our priority is protecting jobs and keeping as much trading as possible. We're monitoring developments, meeting stakeholders and will keep pressing the company and Gordons on their responsibilities.

chapters.title: Debt, directors and possible law changes
chapters.takeaway: Ministers are checking disputed claims about loans, director resignations and special payouts, and say they will review insolvency rules if flaws appear.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There are reports of an asset‑backed loan burden of £30–£60m and of special payouts to Gordon Brothers if the business is liquidated. Do you know the size of the debt or if directors acted wrongly?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: We can't confirm those figures yet—our conversations with the company and the Insolvency Service are ongoing. We're focusing on saving jobs rather than creating extra uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Section 172 currently focuses directors on shareholders. Should director duties be reformed so they must consider wider stakeholders, like workers and communities?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: I'm not alleging misconduct here. If our review of this case shows flaws in the insolvency system or director duties, we'll examine reforms. Right now our immediate action is engagement to protect jobs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does the Government have tools—through the British Business Bank, for example—to help restructure an overly large debt?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: I have confidence in the British Business Bank, but any practical help depends on the specifics; our immediate priority remains pressing the company to prioritise employees and suppliers.

chapters.title: Fireworks — huge public response and enforcement gaps
chapters.takeaway: A wave of public complaints (140,000 consultation responses) has led to proposals to lower fireworks' noise and improve predictability; enforcement and local resourcing remain concerns.

turns.speaker: Antonia Bance
turns.text: Constituents, veterans, pet owners and farmers are exhausted by year‑round, unpredictable fireworks. How will you act on the consultation?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: We launched the first major fireworks review in over 20 years and have received over 140,000 responses. The consultation looks at noise levels, predictability and misuse, and we will analyse responses quickly.

turns.speaker: Sophie George
turns.text: Early trends show most respondents want lower noise and better predictability. Businesses raised concerns about industry impacts; we're still analysing the full evidence, including employment and turnover.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Can changes be implemented quickly enough for the next firework season, and will you need primary legislation?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: Our ambition is to make changes before the next season where possible. Many measures could be taken by secondary legislation, but we must properly analyse the many responses first.

turns.speaker: Sarah Edwards
turns.text: Enforcement is a big problem: police and trading standards are stretched and people feel powerless. Could smartphone videos be accepted as evidence, as has been done for fly‑tipping?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: Yes — we're looking at ways technology helps enforcement. But effective outcomes need properly resourced local enforcement (police, trading standards) and clearer duties on suppliers and users.

chapters.title: Black Friday, misleading prices and CMA enforcement
chapters.takeaway: The CMA is using new powers to crack down on fake discounts and drip pricing but officials want clearer rules (reference‑price timeframes) and faster government action before Christmas.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We heard alarming examples of fake discounts and missing retailers at today's session. Emma, how extensive is the Black Friday problem and what is the CMA doing?

turns.speaker: Emma Cochrane
turns.text: Since our stronger powers came in April 2025 we've opened 20 investigations, closed 7, levied about £12m in fines and ordered redress. We target misleading countdowns, drip pricing and default extras; pricing harms are a very big problem.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: £12m in fines sounds small given the scale of consumer harm. Why so modest?

turns.speaker: Emma Cochrane
turns.text: Our fining policy considers turnover, culpability and harm. Many firms settle, which reduces penalties to reflect administrative savings and lets us pursue more enforcement quickly.

turns.speaker: Mr Reynolds
turns.text: The Government promised an autumn consultation on fake prices and RRPs in August. Black Friday is three weeks away. When will this consultation launch and will it protect shoppers this Christmas?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: We need clear rules so enforcers can act without grey areas. Officials are finalising a draft and clearing it; Tony can explain the details and timing.

turns.speaker: Tony Thomas
turns.text: There's a draft consultation in clearance. It aims to set how long a reference price must have existed (for example, 30 or 60 days) so discounts can't be faked by temporary price hikes or cherry‑picking.

turns.speaker: Mr Reynolds
turns.text: Will this stop cat‑and‑mouse actions—big retailers removing flagged offers then repeating tactics with different products?

turns.speaker: Tony Thomas
turns.text: The goal is to give enforcers like the CMA and trading standards clear rules to prosecute breaches without having to prove intent in every case.

chapters.title: Payments, marketplaces and online scams
chapters.takeaway: Open banking pay‑by‑bank raises protection gaps (no section 75/chargeback); Treasury is consulting on payments while Ministers push for duties on marketplaces and quicker coordination to fight scams.

turns.speaker: Mr Reynolds
turns.text: Pay‑by‑bank via open banking is widespread but lacks section 75 and chargeback protections. Consumers don't realise this. Will Government act?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: The Treasury ran a payments consultation (July–October). Payments innovation must include consumer protections. Treasury leads on these reforms, and we'll work with them to ensure safeguards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could all this be pulled into a single consumer protection plan—a 'one front door'—so people know where to go and the system is joined up?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: Yes. We're developing a consumer action plan, bringing regulators and departments together, looking at Citizens Advice, enforcement pathways and intelligence sharing to simplify the consumer journey.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: And online marketplaces—what duties are you proposing?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: We consulted on world‑leading duties requiring marketplaces to take proactive steps to stop dangerous products, carry out due diligence on sellers and cooperate with regulators to protect consumers.

chapters.title: Product safety: e‑bikes, batteries and furniture
chapters.takeaway: Ministers plan targeted action on illegal or unsafe e‑bikes and are reviewing furniture fire rules to reduce harmful flame retardants while protecting jobs and fire safety.

turns.speaker: Antonia Bance
turns.text: Illegal e‑bikes and conversion kits are a menace in communities. Can you use the Product Regulation and Metrology Act to designate them unsafe and stop their sale?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: We're considering options. OPSS already removes dangerous e‑bikes and batteries from the market. We want targeted action on illegal conversions and unsafe batteries while keeping lawful e‑bike use safe.

turns.speaker: Graham Russell
turns.text: OPSS has been working with local enforcement to seize dangerous e‑bikes and batteries and is contributing to the product safety reform package that will set clearer rules and powers.

turns.speaker: Antonia Bance
turns.text: Link this to employment‑status reform so employers cannot dodge health and safety responsibilities by misclassifying riders.

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: I'll take that link away; it's a sensible point.

turns.speaker: Antonia Bance
turns.text: One more: furniture—constituency manufacturers fear proposals will open the market to lower‑safety competition and cost jobs. Why change furniture fire safety?

turns.speaker: Kate Dearden
turns.text: We consulted on domestic upholstered furniture to keep high fire safety while reducing harmful chemical flame retardants. We are carefully analysing scientific evidence and industry impacts and will meet affected firms.

turns.speaker: Sophie George
turns.text: The proposals are evidence‑based and aim to balance chemical exposures against fire risk; responses from businesses and fire services are being reviewed.
